translations.text: The words of Qoheleth, son of David, king of Jerusalem.
Utter futility, says Qoheleth, utter futility! Everything is futile.
What does a person gain from all the work at which he toils under the sun?
One generation goes and another generation comes, but the earth remains forever.
The sun rises and the sun sets, and it returns to the place where it rises, to rise again from there.
The wind goes south and turns north. Round and round it turns as it goes, and the wind returns to its circuits.
All rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is not filled. To the place where the rivers go, there they return to flow again.
All words are wearying. A person is never satisfied with speaking; the eye is never satisfied with seeing, and the ear is never filled with hearing.
What has happened is what happens, and what has been done is what is done. There is nothing new under the sun.
Whatever someone may speak of and say, “Look, this is new,” already existed in the ages before us.
Those who came before are not remembered. Nor will those who come afterward be remembered by those who come still later.
I, Qoheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I applied my heart to searching and examining with wisdom everything done under the sun. The Lord has given human beings a painful task to occupy themselves with.
I saw every deed done under the sun, and look, everything is futile and a distress to the spirit.
What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be made complete.
I spoke to myself, saying, “Look, I have grown great and gained more wisdom than all who were before me in Jerusalem. My heart has experienced much wisdom and knowledge.”
I applied my heart to knowing wisdom and knowledge, proverbs and foolishness. I learned that this too is distress of spirit.
For with much wisdom comes much frustration, and whoever increases knowledge increases pain.
I said to myself, “Come, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy good things.” But look, this too is futile.
Of laughter I said, “What use is it?” And to pleasure, “What have you accomplished?”

I considered in my heart how to delight my body with wine, while my heart pursued wisdom, and how to take hold of foolishness, until I could see what was good for human beings to do under the sun during the numbered days of their lives.
I increased my works. I built houses for myself and planted vineyards for myself.
I made gardens and parks for myself and planted in them trees bearing every kind of fruit.
I made pools of water for myself to irrigate from them a forest of growing trees.
I acquired male and female slaves, and I had many slaves born in my household. I also owned more cattle and sheep than all who were before me in Jerusalem.

I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the treasures of kings and cities. I provided myself with male and female singers and the pleasures people enjoy. I provided myself with male and female cupbearers.
I became great and increased beyond everyone who had been before me in Jerusalem, and my wisdom also remained with me.
Whatever my eyes desired, I did not withhold from them. I did not keep my heart from any joy, because my heart rejoiced in all my labor. This was my share from all my labor.
I looked at all the work my hands had done and all the labor I had put into doing it. Look, everything was emptiness and distress of spirit, and there was no gain under the sun.
I turned to examine wisdom, madness, and foolishness. For who is the man who can come after the king in judgment? Then with the one who made him [?].
I saw that wisdom has an advantage over foolishness, just as light has an advantage over darkness.
The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I knew that the same fate happens to them all.
I said in my heart, “If the same fate that befalls the fool will also befall me, why have I become so very wise?” And I said in my heart that this too is emptiness.

For the fool talks too much. Neither the wise person nor the fool will be remembered forever, since in the days already approaching everything will be forgotten. How can the wise person die along with the fool!
I hated life, because the work done under the sun was grievous to me, for everything is emptiness and distress of spirit.
I hated all the labor I had done under the sun, because I must leave it to the person who comes after me.
Who knows whether he will be wise or foolish? Yet he will control everything I worked for and accomplished with wisdom under the sun. This too is emptiness.
I turned to giving my heart over to despair about all the labor I had done under the sun.
For someone may labor with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, yet give his share to someone who has not worked for it. This too is emptiness and a great evil.
For what does a person gain from all his labor and the desires of his heart for which he labors under the sun?
For all his days are pain, and his occupation is frustration. Even at night his heart does not rest. This too is futility.
There is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and let himself enjoy good things through his labor. I saw that this too comes from the hand of the Lord.
For who can eat, and who can drink, apart from him?

For to the person who is good in his sight, he gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy. But to sinners he gives the task of accumulating and gathering, only to give it to the one who is good before the Lord. This too is emptiness and distress of spirit.
There is a time for everything, and a time for every activity under the sun.
A time to give birth and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what is planted.
A time to kill and a time to bring to life; a time to tear down and a time to build.
A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance.
A time to throw stones away and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing.
A time to lose and a time to seek; a time to bind and a time to untie.
A time to tear and a time to sew; a time to be silent and a time to speak.
A time to love and a time to hate; a time for war and a time for peace.
What does a person gain from the work at which he toils under the sun?
I saw the task that the Lord has given human beings to occupy themselves with.
Everything he has made is beautiful in its time. He has also put toil in their hearts, so that people cannot discover the work the Lord has done from beginning to end.
I knew that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good during their lives.
Also, that everyone should eat and drink and enjoy good things in all their toil—this is the Lord's gift.
I know that everything the Lord does will last forever. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing can be taken away from it. The Lord has done this so that people will fear him.
What has been already exists, and whatever will be has been long ago. God seeks out the persecuted person who is being pursued.
Again I saw under the sun: in the place of judgment, wickedness was there, and in the place of righteousness, injustice was there.
I said in my heart, “God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every deed there.”
I said in my heart concerning human speech that God created them and would show that they are like animals.

The fate of human beings and the fate of animals comes upon them alike; one fate befalls them all. As one dies, so the other dies, and they all have the same breath. Human beings have no advantage over animals, because everything is futile.
All go to one place. All came from dust, and all return to dust.
Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes upward, and the spirit of animals goes downward to the earth?
I saw that there is nothing better for them than for a person to rejoice in his work, because that is his portion. For who will bring him to see everything that will happen after him?

Again I looked at all the acts of oppression committed under the sun. There were the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter. Power was in the hands of their oppressors, and they had no one to help them.
And I praised the dead, who have already died, more than the living, who are still alive.
But better than both of these is the one who has not yet come into being, because he has not seen the evil work done under the sun.
I saw all toil and all skill in work: they arise from a person's envy of his neighbor. This too is futility and vexation of spirit.
The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.
Better one handful of rest than two handfuls of toil and distress of spirit.
I turned again and saw futility under the sun.

There is someone who is alone, with no companion; he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with wealth. Yet for whom am I toiling and depriving myself of good things? This too is futility and a miserable occupation.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.
For if one falls, his companion lifts him up. But woe to someone who is alone: if he falls, there is no one to lift him up.
If two lie down together, they will keep warm. But how can one keep warm alone?
If one person attacks, the two will stand against him, and a three-stranded cord is not quickly broken.
A poor but wise youth is better than an old, foolish king who no longer knows how to heed a warning.
For he came out of prison to become king, though he was born poor even in his own kingdom.
I saw all the living who walk under the sun siding with the second young man, who would take his place.
There was no end to all the people, to all who were before him. Yet those who come afterward will not rejoice in him either, because this too is futility and vexation of spirit.
Watch your step when you go to the house of God. Drawing near to listen is better than the sacrificial offerings of fools, because they do not know how to do good.
Do not be hasty with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth; therefore let your words be few.
For a dream comes through much activity, and a fool's voice through many words.
When you make a vow to God, do not delay fulfilling it, because he takes no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.
It is better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it.
Do not let your mouth cause your body to sin, and do not say before God, “It was my mistake,” lest God become angry at your words and destroy the work of your hands.
For amid many dreams, empty things, and many words, you must fear God.
If you see oppression of the poor, plunder, and judgment in a province, do not be astonished at the matter. For one higher than the high official is watching, and there are higher ones over them.
The land's produce is for everyone; the king has the field cultivated.
Whoever loves money will not be satisfied with money, and whoever loves wealth will not find it enough. This too is futility.
When goods increase, those who consume them increase. What benefit does their owner have except to look at them with his eyes?
A worker's sleep is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but a rich person's fullness does not let him sleep.
There is a sickening evil that I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his own harm.
That wealth is lost through a bad venture. He has fathered a son, but has nothing in his hand.
As he came out of his mother's womb naked, so he will return, departing as he came. He will take nothing from his toil that he can carry away in his hand.
This too is a grievous affliction: just as he came, so he goes. What profit does he have from all his toil for the wind?
Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, with much anger, fury, mourning, sickness, and fury.

This is what I, the Teacher, have seen: it is good and fitting to eat and drink and enjoy good things in all the toil with which a person toils under the sun during the numbered days of his life that the Lord has given him, because this is his portion.
Moreover, when the Lord gives anyone wealth and possessions and enables him to eat from them, receive his portion, and rejoice in his toil, this too is a gift of God.
For he will not dwell much on the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily on human beings.

There is a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all he desires, yet God does not enable him to eat from it. Instead, a stranger consumes it after him. This is futility and sorrow.

If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are numerous, but his soul is not satisfied with good things and he does not even receive a burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.
For it comes in futility and goes away in darkness, and its name is covered in darkness.
It has neither seen the sun nor known anything, yet it has more rest than that man.
Even if he lives a thousand years twice over but sees no good, does not everyone go to one place?
All a person's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.
For the wise person has an advantage over the fool. What does it profit the poor person to know how to conduct himself among the living?
What the eyes see is better than the wandering of desire. This too is futility and distress of spirit.
Whatever has come into being was named long ago, and it is known that he is human and cannot contend with one stronger than himself.
For there are many words that increase futility. What advantage does a person gain?
For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the numbered days of his futile life, which he passes like a shadow? Who can tell a person what will happen after him under the sun?
A good name is better than fine oil, and the day of death is better than the day of birth.
It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, because this is the end of all human beings, and the living person gains something good for his heart.
Anger is better than laughter, because a sad face makes the heart better.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of rejoicing.
It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to be someone who listens to the song of fools.
For the laughter of fools is like the crackling of thorns under a pot. This too is futility.
For oppression destroys the wise person, and a bribe destroys the heart.
The end of a matter is better than its beginning, and patience is better than pride.
Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the lap of fools.
Do not say, “Why were the former days better than these?” For it is not out of wisdom that you ask about these things.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and it is of greater benefit to those who see the sun.
For the shelter of wisdom is like the shelter of money, but the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to its possessor.
Look at the work of God, for who can straighten what he has made crooked?
On a day of prosperity, enjoy yourself, and on a day of adversity, examine yourself. God has made the one as well as the other, so that a person cannot discover anything that will come after him.
I have seen everything in the days of my fleeting life: there is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked person who lives long in his wickedness.
Do not be excessively righteous, and do not be overly wise, lest you become bewildered.
Do not be very wicked, lest you be greatly hated. Do not be a fool, lest you die before your time.
It is good to hold on to this and not let go of that either, because whoever fears God holds to them all.
Wisdom strengthens the wise more than ten rulers who are in a city.
For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins.
Do not pay attention to everything wicked people say, so that you do not hear your servant insulting you.
For your heart knows that many times you too have insulted others.
I tested all these things by wisdom. I said, “I will become wise,” but wisdom was far from me.
Far beyond everything that exists, and deeper than the depths—who can find it?
I turned, I and my heart, to know, investigate, and seek wisdom and understanding, and to know the wickedness of the fool, foolishness, and madness.

I found something more bitter than death: the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. Whoever is good—whoever is good before God—escapes from her, but whoever sins is caught by her.
“Look, this is what I found,” says the Teacher, “examining one thing after another to find an explanation.
I continued searching, but did not find it. I found one man among a thousand, but among them all I did not find a woman.
But look, this is what I found: God made human beings upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”
Who is like the wise person, and who knows the interpretation of a matter? A person's wisdom lights up his face, and someone whose face is brazen will be hated.
Obey the king's command because of the oaths made to God.
Do not be in a hurry to leave his presence, and do not persist in an evil matter, because he does whatever he wishes.
For when the king speaks, he has authority, and who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
Whoever keeps the command will experience no harm, and the heart of the wise knows the time and the judgment.
For every matter has a time and a judgment, though a person's trouble weighs heavily upon him.
For no one knows what will happen, and who can tell him what will happen after him?

No one has power over the spirit to restrain the spirit, and there is no authority over the day of death. There is no escape on the day of battle, and wickedness will not rescue those who practice it.
I saw all this and applied my heart to understanding every deed done under the sun, and the time when one person rules over another to harm him.
Then I saw wicked people who were buried and were coming, and they went away from the holy place and were forgotten in the city where they had acted this way. This too is futility.
Because punishment is not quickly exacted from those who do evil, people's hearts are filled with the desire to do evil.
Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives long, I know that it will be well with those who fear the Lord, who stand in fear before him.
But it will not be well with the wicked person, nor will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear God.

There is a futility that occurs on earth: there are righteous people who receive what the deeds of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked people who receive what the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is futility.

I praised joy, because there is nothing better for a person under the sun than to eat, drink, and be glad. This accompanies him in his labor throughout all the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
For this reason I applied my heart to knowing wisdom and observing the activity carried on upon the earth, because neither by day nor by night does a person find sleep for his eyes.

I saw all the work of God: a person cannot comprehend the work done under the sun. However hard a person labors to seek it out, he will not find it. Even if a wise person claims to know, he cannot discover it.
For I took all these things to heart, and my heart saw all this: the righteous, the wise, and their deeds are in God's hand. A person knows neither love nor hatred. Everything before him is futility.

Everything is alike for everyone. One fate comes to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the person who offers sacrifices and the person who does not. As it is with the good person, so it is with the sinner; as it is with the person who swears an oath, so it is with the person who fears taking oaths.

This is an evil in everything done under the sun: one fate comes to everyone. Moreover, the human heart is filled with evil, and wicked madness is in their hearts and in their lives. Their end is among the dead.
For anyone who is joined to all the living, there is hope, because a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They no longer have any reward, because their memory has been forgotten.
Their love, their hatred, and their jealousy have already perished. They will never again have a share in anything done under the sun.
Come, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, because God has approved your deeds.
Let your clothes always be white, and let oil never be lacking on your head.
Enjoy life with the woman you love throughout all the days of your fleeting life, because this is your share in life and in the labor at which you toil under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength, because there is no work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom in Sheol, where you are going.

Again I saw under the sun that the race does not belong to the swift, nor the battle to the mighty, nor bread to the wise, nor wealth to the discerning, nor praise to the knowledgeable, because time and chance happen to them all.
For a person does not know his time. Like fish caught in a cruel net and birds caught in a snare, so people are caught in an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.
I also saw this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.
There was a small city with few people in it. A great king came against it, surrounded it, and built siegeworks against it.
A poor, wise man was found in it, and that poor man rescued the city through his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
And I said, “Wisdom is better than strength, yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.”
The words of the wise spoken quietly are heeded more than the shouting of a ruler among fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sin destroys many good things.
Dead flies make a container of fragrant oil stink. A little folly outweighs wisdom and abundant glory.
The wise person's heart is to his right, but the fool's heart is to his left.
Even when a fool walks along the road, he lacks sense, and everything he thinks is foolishness.
If a ruler's anger rises against you, do not leave your place, because laxness produces many sins.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, like an error that occurs in a ruler's presence:
a fool sits in a very high position, while the rich sit in lowly places.
I saw slaves on horses, and rulers walking on the ground like slaves.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall will be bitten by a snake.
Whoever moves stones will be hurt by them, and whoever splits wood will grow tired from it.
If the iron grows dull, it disfigures faces and increases the number of those killed; but wisdom is an advantage to the skillful.
If a snake bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage in the charmer.
The words from a wise person's mouth bring praise, but a fool's lips drown him.
The beginning of the words from his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his speech is wicked shamelessness.
A fool multiplies words. No one knows what will happen, and who can tell him what will happen after him?
The toil of fools wears them out, because they do not know how to get to the city.
Woe to you, city whose king is a child and whose officials eat in the morning!
Happy are you, city, whose king is of noble birth and whose rulers eat at the proper time, with discipline and not in drunkenness.
Through laziness the roof sags, and through idle hands the house leaks.
Bread, wine, and oil are prepared for joy, to gladden the living; but money humbles them and leads them astray in everything.
Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, and do not curse the rich in your bedroom, because a bird of the sky will carry your voice, and a winged creature will report your words.
Send your bread out over the surface of the water, because after many days you will find it.
Give a share to seven, and even to eight, because you do not know what disaster will happen on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they will pour it onto the earth. Whether a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, wherever the tree falls, there it will remain.
Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.
Just as you do not know the path of the wind or how a woman conceives, so you do not know the works of the Lord, all that he does.
Sow your seed every morning, and do not let your hand rest in the evening, because you do not know which will succeed, this one or that one, or whether both will be equally good.
Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
For if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, and let him remember the days of darkness, because they will be many. Everything that comes is fleeting.
Rejoice, young man, in the days of your youth, and enjoy yourself. Follow the ways of your heart and what your eyes see, but know that for all these things the Lord will bring you to judgment.
Remove anger from your heart and keep harm away from your body, because youth and ignorance are a passing breath.
Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years approach when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them.”
Before the sun and the light of the moon and stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain.
On the day when the keepers of the house tremble, the strong men become unsteady, the grinding women stop because they are few, and those looking through the windows grow dim;
when the doors to the street are shut, when the sound of the grinding women grows faint, when one rises at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low;

when one is afraid of heights and trembles on the roads, sleeplessness comes upon him, the [?] blossoms, the locust grows, the caper is scattered, and desire ceases, because a person goes to the house of his toil, and dancers go around in the streets;
before the silver cord is cut, the golden apple is crushed, the pitcher is broken at the spring, and the wheel runs over the well.
And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to the Lord who gave it.
“Utter futility,” says Qoheleth, “utter futility! Everything is futile.”
Besides being wise, Qoheleth taught the people knowledge. He listened, investigated, and arranged many proverbs.
Qoheleth searched diligently to find pleasing words, and he wrote honestly, using words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads and like firmly fixed nails. The masters of [?] were given by one shepherd.
Beyond these, my son, be warned: there is no end to writing many books, and much speaking wearies the body.
The conclusion of the matter in its entirety: hear everything, fear the Lord, and keep his commandments, because this is what has been given to everyone by one craftsman.
For the Lord will bring every deed into judgment, everything hidden and revealed, whether good or evil.
